summary: TERRA-X is an open web app and physics engine that answers one operational question for the Artemis era: where on Earth can a solar-powered lunar south pole base be rehearsed, which conditions transfer, which do not, and what must be measured on the ground first? At the pole the Sun never rises above 7 degrees, so grazing light, long shadows and very long nights decide whether a rover or a base survives. TERRA-X computes these conditions deterministically from real NASA data: LRO/LOLA relief of Mons Mouton at 60 m and Sun positions from SPICE/DE421 kernels, checked against JPL Horizons to 0.00001 degrees on the Moon. On flat ground a parked rover faces 289 to 418 hours of darkness per lunation, 6 to 8 times the 50 hour battery limit of a VIPER-class rover, and in the 30 x 30 km of relief we studied no spot stays under that limit, so a rover there must move or carry more energy. Users explore the real terrain in 3D with a moving Sun, park a rover and follow power and battery hour by hour, and compare the Moon and the Earth under the same Sun angle. Earth candidate sites are still demonstration data and are labelled as such in the app.
details:
WHAT IT DOES
TERRA-X helps mission planners and students decide where on Earth a lunar south pole operation can be rehearsed. The Moon side is computed from real NASA data. The Earth side is a framework that compares candidate terrains property by property (horizon profile, slope, roughness, grazing-light response) and states what transfers, what does not, and what must be measured on site.
MAIN VIEWS
Home: the real relief of Mons Mouton (84.60 S, 31.00 E) in 3D from LOLA data at 60 m, with the shadows of a real lunation moving across it.
3D lab: click anywhere on the relief to park a solar rover, choose the season and the power it needs, and follow Sun elevation, panel power and battery hour by hour. Every attempt is kept in a list so places can be compared.
Safe havens: a map of where darkness stays under the 50 hour battery survival limit of a VIPER-class rover. In the 30 x 30 km crop of Mons Mouton we studied, none of the terrain qualifies in either season: the median longest darkness is 407 h in the summer lunation and 501 h in winter (on a flat horizon the night would last 289 to 418 h). The finding is that a parked rover is lost there unless it travels or carries more energy.
Two worlds: the same rover and the same 0.50 m board under the same Sun angle on the Moon and on Earth, with live shadow length, panel power, a gravity drop test and the time a grazing Sun lasts.
Candidate comparator and field kit: up to three candidates side by side, and a field kit to type a shadow measured on the ground and check it against the Sun model.
Verification: an open report of every test, source file and SHA-256 hash. Tests that have not been run are shown as pending, never as passed.
HOW IT WORKS
A deterministic Python engine (folder motor/) computes horizons with curvature, the Sun position (Skyfield with the DE421 ephemeris in the Moon mean-Earth frame, checked against JPL Horizons), rover power and battery, the safe-haven map and analog scores. A small server wraps the engine for live calculation. The browser repeats the same formulas over the exported files, so the app also works offline, and it always states which path produced each result. No model computes any number: results are reproducible (same inputs give the same SHA-256) and the browser calculation stays within 5 percent of the engine.
BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT
Terrestrial analog sites are often chosen with incomplete characterization. TERRA-X makes the argument explicit and checkable: which physical conditions a site must share with the lunar pole, how far a candidate departs from them, and which field measurement would close the gap. It is open source (Apache-2.0), bilingual (English and Spanish), keyboard accessible, works on a phone and works offline after the first visit.
TOOLS
TypeScript, React, Vite, three.js, Python (NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, pyproj, Skyfield), Blender for the 3D models, Playwright and axe-core for browser and accessibility checks, pytest, Vercel for hosting. Source code: https://github.com/gadielvera12954/NASA-TERRAX
WHAT IS REAL AND WHAT IS NOT YET
Real: the LOLA relief of Mons Mouton, the Sun model (0.00001 degree agreement with JPL Horizons on the Moon), the lunar illumination check against NASA's average-visibility map (correlation 0.99), the rover power and battery model and the safe-haven map.
Not yet: the Earth candidate sites and controls are demonstration data (marked MOCK DATA in the app). Earth terrain grids from NASADEM and Copernicus were not integrated in time, although the ingest code exists. In the published validation report 9 of 17 tests pass and 8 are pending (field shadow measurement, real footprint distributions, tests with people). The colours of the ground and sky in the Two Worlds view and the generic rover shape are illustrative and labelled as such.
USE OF SI (SUPER INTELLIGENCE)
Code, documentation and tests were written with the help of SI coding tools: Claude Code (Anthropic), Codex (OpenAI) and the Antigravity coding assistant. Every file written with SI states it in its header or metadata, and the full declaration is in SI_USAGE.md in the repository. Team members reviewed the code and ran the test suites. No SI model computes any physical result: the numbers come from the deterministic engine and published NASA data. Generated content contains no NASA logos, flags or mission identifiers.

NAIF SPICE kernels (DE421 ephemeris, lunar frame and orientation kernels)
LRO LOLA south polar elevation models, PGDA product 90 (LDEM_80S_20MPP_ADJ, LDEM_60S_60MPP_ADJ, LDEM_60S_240MPP_ADJ)
Lunar polar average solar illumination, PGDA product 69 (AVGVISIB_85S_060M_201608)
NASA VIPER mission (public rover dimensions and 50 h battery survival figure)
